Unreal Cushioning

Our Dynamic Air system features dual-chambered tubes with tuned pressure levels. This means airflow shifts within each set of tubes in response to compression, providing a custom cushioning experience.


Unreal Motion

The Dynamic Air system sits directly on top of the rubber outsole to get you as close to the ground as possible for smoother transition. Plush foam is placed underfoot for additional comfort.


Unreal Flow

Sculpted upper is made of lightweight mesh on top, while slashes at the sides reveal open mesh for more breathability. Design lines help radiate energy throughout your look.

properties.body: Brooklyn is home to everyone from everywhere. My name is Nicole. I'm from Brooklyn, New York. I'm a content creator, a client advisor, a stylist, and I'm a creative.

Brooklyn style means unlocking a new character every day. I grew up in Flatbush first before I move to Canarsie. We're forever evolving around in Brooklyn. When you go out and you see different people that kind of inspires you, whether you're...

...from one neighborhood or the other. When I went to high school is kind of where I emerged into being who I am. That was the star of the show. That was where we were wearing platform shoes, platform heels. That was the time you put on a fit.

The way I would wear something is not the same way the next person would wear it. So when it comes to styling, I have to try to find pieces for certain artists or people that kind of match their style, but kind of have my twist to it.
I'm not contained to just one style. One day I could be sporty. The other day I could be girly. I could do street wear. It's kind of unnatural to feel comfortable in a community that's forever...
...evolving. My nails is a big piece of my stylin' now. When you go around Brooklyn, you have all these beauty supply stores that has press on. They even have crazy nail designs as well.
I think as a woman, your nails kind of tell a story, but it's a simple French that's the classy, your classy, cutesy girl. It kind of shows personality to me...
...and how bright and vibrant I can be. There's so many different people around you to even shape you as a human being.
Overall. That's one thing I could say about everybody from Brooklyn. We kind of want to see each other grow, whether it's 10 years later, we all still come back and support each other.
Even if it comes to moving out of New York or getting out of Brooklyn, it's the fact that you started there. At the end of the day, I'm from Brooklyn.

properties.body: New York moves how it wants. It's fast, unrelenting, but also beautiful. The rhythm of the court, of color, of the street, the way I paint, the way I play...
...it's how I move and it's what I make. My name is Andrea Bergart and I'm an artist and designer in New York City.

I love how intuitive basketball is. I love how fun it's always been for me. More recently, it's been embedded into my studio practice and my design practice, which seems pretty natural since I've always been interested in it.
There's a great improvisation that happens in basketball where you're responding to your teammates and yourself in space on the court, and I try to bring that into my artwork as well.

Some of my paintings require more structure and very much being in the flow and sort of leaning into the qualities of the paint. I think there's a lot of personal movement and signature styles in basketball that I love.
How you play basketball and how you dress. I think that's directly relates to how you want to express yourself.
I'm drawn to the figures in basketball. I think that to me, I'm interested in unique gestures that happen on the court and then extending those or exaggerating those.
It's pretty exciting to design and then to paint a 50 foot painting. Exciting to have people play on a painting where you're not normally supposed to be touching artwork.
It's taking more of a presence in my life for sure. I still play, it's in my designs, it's in my paintings, so it's taking the main stage now.

properties.body: It was the summer of ‘85, a 22-year-old MJ went on a European tour. London, Paris, and, for some reason, Trieste, Italy where he shattered the basketball universe.
Signore e signori. From the City of Wind, Chicago, Michael Jordan! It was supposed to be a friendly exhibition.
Stoppata! But friendly and exhibition were not in MJ’s vocabulary. Da Due Jordan! Ancora Jordan! Ma che vuoi?Jordan canestro! Jordan da due! Time out. Time out. Jordan, Jordan, Jordan!

properties.altText: The Nike Muse: Q&A with Veneda Carter

content.text: Q: Can you introduce yourself and what do you do?

I’m a designer, stylist, creative, and model. I began my career in front of the camera, starting modeling at 13, which gave me an early understanding of fashion from the inside out. In my 20s, I moved to Los Angeles and transitioned into styling where I discovered my love for shaping stories through clothing. That eventually evolved into designing, beginning with jewelry and now expanding into broader categories - allowing me to bring my own visual language to life. I've also collaborated with other brands on design projects, which has been a natural extension of my creative practice.

properties.altText: The Nike Muse: Q&A with Veneda Carter

content.text: Q: Having grown up in Denmark but spending a lot of time in Warsaw, how did that impact your style?
Veneda:

The intermix between these two cities and cultures has had a huge influence on how I approach style. Denmark gave me a foundation of clean lines, minimalism, and a sense of intentionality. Everything is functional, refined, and understated. In contrast, my time in Warsaw introduced a very different energy— Eastern European style is more raw, bold, and expressive. There's a kind of toughness and edge to it that feels less polished and more instinctive. Blending those two perspectives has definitely shaped my aesthetic. I’m drawn to contrasts: sharp vs soft, structured vs undone, simplicity layered with statement. I think my style lives somewhere in that tension.

content.text: Q: How would you describe your approach and work in the fashion space?
Veneda:

My approach to fashion is rooted in instinct, I feel like I’m drawn to pieces that evoke a feeling before anything else. With styling, I love to play with bold proportions, unexpected silhouettes, and rich textures. I’m constantly exploring how fabric moves and how shape can distort or exaggerate the body. There’s a freedom in dressing that I deeply value and I always aim to balance visual strength with a sense of ease and wearability. I’m interested in building looks that feel lived-in, powerful, and personal.

content.text: Q: How did your love of utilitarian outerwear inspire this colorway? And were there any other inspirations?
Veneda:

I’ve always been drawn to utilitarian design, especially the functional materials and textures that come with it. This palette also ties back to the brutalist architecture of the apartment building in Warsaw where my father grew up and I now own. The bright pink was my way of creating tension. It brings in a layer of sport and femininity— an unexpected contrast that energizes the look.

My favorite part is the reflective green bubbles, they catch light in an unexpected and playful way. And of course, the lace tip. It’s a meaningful detail with my signature jewelry texture which feels like a full circle moment to incorporate into the design.

content.text: Kobe Bryant and Nike unveiled the Kobe X in January of 2015. The design for the tenth signature installment fused three advanced footwear innovations crafted into a minimalist form.

The Kobe X originally released as a low-cut sneaker in an open-weave sharkskin-inspired textile upper, which provided lightweight durability. The hybrid cushioning system combined Lunarlon, Nike Free-inspired siping grooves and a Zoom Air unit. The outsole took insights from intricate treads on performance racecar tires and featured hundreds of tiny “nodules” that grip the court. Delivering maximum grip, natural movement, and firm yet soft responsiveness, the traction and cushioning elements were paired together in a translucent rubber casing.

As part of the Nike Basketball Elite series, the Kobe X Elite later featured a high-cut Flyknit construction and Flywire technology in the upper. Over the course of the year, other colorway narratives introduced a low-cut Flyknit version.

content.text: Kobe Bryant and Nike unveiled the Zoom Kobe V in December of 2009. Doubling down on the innovation of the prior silhouette, this signature model arrived as Nike Basketball’s lowest-profile and lightest basketball shoe at the time of release.

The Kobe V was the result of vigorous testing to ensure lateral stability, mid-foot control and rigidity. Flywire technology was modified to achieve a lighter weight, overlays were bonded with heat welding, and Zoom Air units were added in the heel and forefoot.
The Kobe V was the first in the line to include a codified language sequence known as the Kobe Code, represented through a dotmatrix symbol on the front edge of the outsole.

content.text: Kobe Bryant and Nike unveiled the Kobe VII—also known as the Kobe VII System—in December of 2011. This shoe introduced a customization concept to the signature line, allowing players to interchange the cushioning and ankle support for their style of play.

Two inserts were created, labeled as Attack Fast and Attack Strong. The former was built with speed in mind, and featured a Phylon midsole with Zoom Air units in the forefoot and heel for lightweight responsiveness. Also included was a low-cut, power-stretch cuﬀ that hugs the foot for support. content.text: Kobe Bryant and Nike unveiled the Kobe IX—also known as the Kobe IX Elite—in December of 2013. Recognized as one of Nike Basketball’s most innovative shoes at the time, the ninth signature installment blended key technologies all throughout in a high-cut design.

The upper for the Kobe IX merged Flyknit lightweight engineering—a first for Nike Basketball—and Flywire technology for dynamic lockdown support. Lunarlon technology in the midsole provided responsive cushioning and the durable outsole featured a traction pattern mimicking the natural contours of the foot.

Breaking from the low-cut industry standard that Kobe himself ushered in, the Kobe IX Elite’s high-cut design was more than two years in the making and a result of Kobe’s observations from boxing. A low-cut version of the Kobe IX was later released in both Flyknit and engineered mesh variants.

content.text: Kobe Bryant and Nike unveiled the Zoom Kobe II in December of 2006. The follow up to Kobe’s introductory shoe featured key modifications to deliver another high-performance experience on the court.

The Kobe II kept a full-grain leather upper approach, swapping the prior model’s padded ankle collar for a leather ankle strap. A full-length Zoom Air unit delivered enhanced comfort, while the Phylon midsole was reimagined to allow for range and flexibility. The Herringbone outsole pattern was broken into pods and flex grooves were extended, an early sign of Kobe’s keen interest in improving traction and on-court feel.
